To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

parents reported that their melanoma-susceptible children engaged in parent-assistant SSEs, but the majority of children were not receiving recommended monthly skin self-examinations and only a small proportion of children had received a professional skin exam in the previous 6 months.
parents of melanoma survivors reported that most of their children were engaging in parent-assisted SSEs, but few children were receiving SSEs at the recommended frequency.
parents of children with a familial history of melanoma reported their children engaging in skin self-exams, but the majority of children did not receive skin examinations from a healthcare provider.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prevention and control of melanoma.
the identification of risk factors associated with skin cancer and the development of interventions to promote skin cancer prevention behaviors among children at elevated risk for skin cancer.
the development of a new screening method for melanoma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
children with a family melanoma history may be engaging in skin exams but that more research is needed to better understand the extent of these behaviors.
there is a need for more research on skin screening practices in pediatric populations at elevated risk for melanoma.
there is insufficient research to determine whether skin cancer screening for children with a family or personal history of skin cancer is warranted.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

parents of children with a history of melanoma in the family are engaging their children in skin self-exams and are reporting recommendations from healthcare providers to perform skin exams, yet they are not reporting that they have received guidance on how frequently to perform skin exams.

children of melanoma patients are not currently receiving recommended skin screening practices, and there is a need for more research in this area to develop and test interventions to improve screening behaviors.
children of melanoma patients are engaging in skin screening practices with the help of parents, despite the lack of evidence-based guidelines.
The main takeaway from our work is that
parents of melanoma survivors are engaging in screening practices, but they are not receiving recommendations from healthcare providers.
there are currently no evidence-based guidelines for skin screening in pediatric populations.
children of melanoma patients are engaging in skin screening, despite the lack of evidence on how often to screen.
